walkthroughs.body_html:
Reproduction & Inheritance — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Reproduction & Inheritance brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Reproduction & Inheritance.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: A recessive trait shows only if a person has:
options: one recessive allele
two recessive alleles
one dominant allele
no allele

mcqs.q: What does it mean for an allele to be 'dominant'?
options: A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
It is expressed in the phenotype when at least one copy is present (in a heterozygote).
A dominant allele is the most common allele in a population.

mcqs.q: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more common in males?
options: Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed — there's no second X to mask it.
X-linked conditions affect only males because females cannot inherit X-linked alleles.
X-linked recessive conditions affect more males because the Y chromosome makes the disease worse.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: A dominant allele physically destroys the recessive allele in the genome.
No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.

mcqs.q: Cross Bb × Bb. What ratio of offspring are bb?
A pea plant cross Bb × Bb is carried out. Of 200 offspring, roughly how many are expected to show the recessive phenotype (bb)?
Sexual reproduction produces offspring that vary, but asexual reproduction produces clones. Which best explains the difference?
options: Sexual reproduction combines alleles from two parents.
Asexual reproduction always causes mutations.
Sexual reproduction uses only one parent.
Asexual reproduction mixes two sets of alleles.

mcqs.q: A father is colour-blind (X-linked recessive) and the mother is not a carrier. What is true of their children?
options: Daughters will be carriers; sons will not be colour-blind.
All sons will be colour-blind.
All children will be colour-blind.
All daughters will be colour-blind.

mcqs.q: At fertilisation, a sperm and egg fuse. What is the chromosome number of the zygote compared with each gamete?
options: Double — the diploid number is restored
Half — it stays haploid
The same as one gamete
Four times the gamete number
